name: Freya Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Freya. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no links to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Whatever you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Harlow Board and Box, on the industrial park by the canal. We make cardboard boxes, the brown corrugated kind, for supermarkets and online shops. I run the back end of a folder-gluer, which takes flat printed sheets, folds them, glues the seam and spits them out as flat boxes, and I count them into bundles and watch for bad glue lines. It's sixteen months now, and I still lean on Dave, the main operator, whenever it jams.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's the same every day. I know where my locker is, I know the tea break is ten fifteen, I know the machine. Before this I was a cashier at a bank for eighteen years until the branch closed, so I've had enough surprises. What wears me out is my feet, the concrete floor is murder, and the cardboard dust, which gets in your hair so my daughter Ama says I smell like a parcel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, good, that's one less thing. At work we'd probably just carry on talking about the football and the canteen prices. I don't go online much, maybe the school parents' group, and nobody there would care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I can relax a bit. The bank taught me that the machines come for you in the end, so if they don't come this time, I'll take it. I'd keep my head down and get better at the folder-gluer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd carry on exactly as she is and maybe ask Dave to teach her the setting-up side properly. She'd keep putting a bit by each month on top of the bank redundancy money they still have. Nothing else would change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like when the rain holds off for the barbecue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the machines come for you in the end. Tell me about the bank.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First they put in the cash machines, then the app, then they said fewer people were coming in, which was true because they'd told everyone to use the app. We heard rumours for three years before they closed us. The day itself was almost a relief.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any of the AI tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My son Sam uses one for his homework and I tell him off. I'm not against it for other people, I just don't see what it would do for me, and I'd rather not hand it my business.

S0.say: Well, good, that's one less thing. At work we'd carry on talking about the football and the canteen prices, and nobody in the parents' group would care.
S0.think: It means I can relax a bit, because the bank taught me the machines come for you in the end. If they don't come this time, I'll take it and keep my head down.
S0.do: Carries on as she is at Harlow and asks Dave to teach her the setting-up side of the folder-gluer. Keeps adding a little each month to the bank redundancy savings they still hold.
S0.feel: Calm, like the rain holding off for a barbecue.
S0.quote: We heard rumours for three years before they closed us. The day itself was almost a relief.
S0.fieldNote: Freya's whole view of technology is shaped by watching her bank branch shrink and close after three years of rumours. She values routine above almost everything. She doesn't oppose AI on principle; she simply sees nothing in it for her and keeps her distance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's business, companies will do what saves them money, and you can't really blame them. But they should look after the people who've given them years. I wouldn't make speeches, I'd just say it over tea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be counting the days. Counting bundles is exactly the job a machine could do with a camera, and I'm the newest on the line. I've been here before, and I know what the start of it looks like: a man with a clipboard walking round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd start saving harder straight away, cutting the gym membership and the takeaways. She'd keep an eye on the job board at the other box plants nearby, the one on Station Road especially, and wait to see what Harlow actually brings in. She wouldn't do any course unless Harlow made it part of the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, I think. Not because I'd be broke, we'd manage, but because I'd be back in the waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd manage. How long could you manage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi has his tyre garage, and we've got about fourteen months put by, plus the redundancy money from the bank that we never touched. So the money isn't the fear. The fear is starting somewhere new again, being the slow one again, at forty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd watch the other plants, but you wouldn't do a course. Why one and not the other?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because moving to another box plant is the same job with a different car park. A course means being a beginner at something I don't understand, with young people who are faster than me. I did that once at forty-two, I'd rather not do it at forty-five.

S1.say: It's business, companies will do what saves them money and you can't really blame them. But they should look after people who've given them years, and I'd say that over tea, not in speeches.
S1.think: I'd be counting the days, because counting bundles is a job a camera could do and I'm the newest on the line. I know what the start of it looks like: a man with a clipboard walking round.
S1.do: Cuts the gym membership and takeaways to save harder straight away. Watches job boards at nearby box plants, especially on Station Road, and waits to see what Harlow brings in, doing a course only if it's part of the job.
S1.feel: Anxious, not about money but about being back in the waiting.
S1.quote: I know what the start of it looks like: a man with a clipboard walking round.
S1.fieldNote: Even steady change makes Freya anxious, though her savings are strong; the trigger is memory, not money. She'd rather move sideways to the same job elsewhere than become a beginner again. Her centrist view shows in how she refuses to blame companies while still expecting fairness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to sort this out, because if it's everyone at once, it's not just business any more. People like me did everything right, saved, worked, didn't moan. I'd say it at work and maybe sign a petition, but I'm not a march person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think it's the bank all over again but for the whole town. Kofi's garage too, if robots can change tyres. I'd be scared stiff, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd stop all spending that isn't food, bills or the mortgage, and she'd ask Kofi to hold off on the new tyre machine he wants. She'd sign petitions and write to her representative. She'd stay at Harlow until the last day, because she believes the people who leave early lose their redundancy money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be waking up at three with my heart going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is not much time. Would anything you'd do now be different because it's so close?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay off as much of the mortgage as I could with the bank money, right away. A house you own is a house they can't take. Everything else I'd freeze. I wouldn't try to learn anything, because what would I learn that a robot can't?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ama and Sam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say keep your heads down and work hard, same as always. Ama's fifteen and she's clever, she'd ask me what the point of school is. I don't know what I'd tell her, honestly, I'd probably just say because I said so.

S2.say: The government needs to sort this out, because if it's everyone at once it isn't just business any more. People like me did everything right, saved, worked and didn't moan, and I'd sign a petition but I'm not a march person.
S2.think: It's the bank all over again, but for the whole town, and Kofi's garage too if robots can change tyres. I'd be scared stiff.
S2.do: Freezes all spending except food, bills and the mortgage, and asks Kofi to hold off on a new tyre machine. Uses the bank redundancy money to pay down the mortgage, signs petitions, writes to her representative and stays at Harlow to the last day for her redundancy pay.
S2.feel: Alarmed, waking at three in the morning with her heart racing.
S2.quote: A house you own is a house they can't take.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year picture turns Freya's private fear of repetition into alarm for her whole household, including her partner's garage. Her instinct is to protect, not adapt: pay down the house, freeze spending, stay put. She admits she wouldn't have an answer for her daughter's question about school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for the government to plan, so they'd better. Proper redundancy rules, help with the mortgage for people who lose their jobs. I'd say it calmly, but I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years might be worse for me than two. It's the bank again: years of rumours, everyone watching everyone, wondering who's next. I'd rather it just happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd pay off the mortgage over the five years using the bank money and overpayments, so it's done by about 2030. She'd stay at Harlow and keep her head down, and she'd let Kofi decide about the garage. She wouldn't retrain, but she'd ask Harlow to let her learn the main operator's job, because that's the last person they'd get rid of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed in a slow way. Like a tooth that aches for months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say five years might be worse than two. That's not what most people would say. Can you explain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the bank, the last three years were the worst of my life, and the closing day was nothing. In the fast one, it's a shock and then you deal with it. In this one, I'd be lying awake for five years. Kofi says I'm daft, but he didn't work there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd learn the main operator's job. Isn't that a kind of retraining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, it's the same machine, just the front end instead of the back. I know Dave, I know the noises it makes. That's not starting again, that's moving three metres to the left.

S3.say: Five years is enough time for the government to plan, so they'd better, with proper redundancy rules and help with mortgages for people who lose their jobs. I'd say it calmly, but I'd mean it.
S3.think: Five years might be worse for me than two, because it's the bank again: years of rumours and everyone wondering who's next. I'd rather it just happened.
S3.do: Pays off the mortgage by about 2030 using the bank money and overpayments. Stays at Harlow and asks to learn the main operator's job on the same folder-gluer, but doesn't retrain, and leaves the garage decision to Kofi.
S3.feel: A slow alarm, like a tooth that aches for months.
S3.quote: That's not starting again, that's moving three metres to the left.
S3.fieldNote: Freya flips the usual logic: for her, more warning means more years of dread, because that's how the bank closure felt. She'd accept learning within her own machine but sees anything wider as starting over, which she won't do. Her mood stays at alarmed, driven by memory rather than money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and a lot can happen, so let's not panic yet. I'd say the government should start working on it now, so it's not a mess when it comes. That's about as political as I get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, by ten years I'd be fifty-three, the house paid, the kids grown or at university. That helps. But it's still ten years of the man with the clipboard, and I don't know if I can do that again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd keep working at Harlow, pay the mortgage off early and build up savings for the kids' studies. She'd tell herself not to worry until there's something to worry about, and wait for Harlow to make the first move. If it came to it around year eight, she'd go and work in Kofi's garage on the front desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's further off, so I can push it to the back most days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've mentioned Kofi's garage now. Would you really work there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be good on the front desk, I did eighteen years with customers at the bank. Kofi would drive me mad, and I'd drive him mad. But it's family, and if the robots come, family is what you've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would anything make you learn something new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Kofi's garage needed someone who understood the booking system, I'd learn it for him. Not for a stranger, not for a certificate. I'd learn it for the family, slowly, with Sam laughing at me.

S4.say: Ten years is a long time and a lot can happen, so let's not panic yet. The government should start working on it now so it isn't a mess when it comes.
S4.think: By then I'd be fifty-three with the house paid and the kids grown, which helps. But it's still ten years of the man with the clipboard, and I don't know if I can do that again.
S4.do: Keeps working at Harlow, pays off the mortgage early and saves for the children's studies. Waits for Harlow to move first and, around year eight, would move to the front desk at Kofi's tyre garage if needed.
S4.feel: Anxious, but far enough off to push to the back of her mind most days.
S4.quote: If the robots come, family is what you've got.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years softens Freya but doesn't settle her, because long warnings remind her of the drawn-out bank closure. Her only plan B is family: the front desk at her partner's garage, where she'd learn new software for him but not for a stranger. Her paid-off house is her anchor in every picture.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The five-year one, I think, even though everyone else probably says the fast one. Five years of waiting is the bank again, and I can't do that twice. What would help is someone being straight with us early, a date and a plan, instead of rumours, and proper redundancy money for people who stayed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask why I chose a factory after the bank. It's because I thought a box is a box, you can't send a box through an app. And now you're telling me a robot can fold it. I'm not angry, I'm just tired of being right about machines.

headlineQuote: I'm not angry, I'm just tired of being right about machines.
portrait: Freya Mensah is 43 and has worked at the back end of a folder-gluer at Harlow Board and Box for sixteen months, after eighteen years as a bank cashier until her branch closed. She lives with her partner Kofi, who runs a tyre garage, and two children, and they hold strong savings, including untouched bank redundancy money. She prizes routine, never uses AI and doesn't blame companies, but three years of closure rumours left a deep mark. She's calm only if AI fizzles, anxious with steady change, and alarmed by AGI in two or five years, finding the longer wait almost worse; with ten years she's anxious, paying off the house and falling back on family.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2031, because five years of waiting would feel like the drawn-out bank closure all over again.
whatWouldHelp: Someone being straight early with a date and a plan instead of rumours, and proper redundancy money for those who stayed.
